title: James Wang
text: My name is James and I am part of the UBC MDS cohort of 26/27. I’ve recently completed my Bachelor of Science in Environmental Sciences in 2026 and I’m now attending the UBC MDS program. I am hoping to combine my domain expertise in Environmental Science with the technical expertise from MDS to land an environmental analytics role after graduation.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Orientation week kicked off with meeting the rest of my cohort, starting with the people at my orientation table. After the formal sessions wrapped up, a few of us grabbed ice cream nearby, which turned out to be a great way to start putting names to faces before classes even began.
The first week of actual classes was a lot to take in. Between new course content and figuring out how everything gets submitted, I felt a bit overwhelmed at times. That said, I managed to get through all my assignments for the week, which felt like a solid first win.
Heading into the next week, I’m shifting focus toward prepping for upcoming quizzes. It’s a good reminder that MDS moves fast, so staying a little ahead rather than catching up after the fact will probably be the theme for the rest of the term.

title: Penguins in Python
text:
Analysis
In this post, I will examine whether the three penguin species in the Palmer Archipelago differ in size. The Palmer Penguins dataset contains 344 records of penguins from three species across three Antarctic islands, which I will use to compare their body mass. Below I import the necessary libraries and load the dataset:

Each row is one penguin. The columns record its species, island, bill and flipper measurements, body mass in grams, sex, and the year it was measured.

print(f"Rows before cleaning: {len(penguins)}")
print(penguins["body_mass_g"].isna().sum(), "rows are missing body mass")
clean = penguins.dropna(subset=["body_mass_g"])
print(f"Rows after cleaning: {len(clean)}")

Rows before cleaning: 344
2 rows are missing body mass
Rows after cleaning: 342


Because two penguins have no body mass recorded, I dropped them. Everything below uses the remaining 342 penguins.

summary = (
    clean
    .groupby("species")["body_mass_g"]
    .agg(["count", "mean", "std"])
    .round(1)
)

Gentoo penguins are clearly the heaviest, averaging about 5,076 g. Adelie and Chinstrap penguins are much lighter and very similar to each other, at roughly 3,700 g and 3,733 g. That means a typical Gentoo is around 1,300 g, or about a third, heavier than the other two species.

species = sorted(clean["species"].unique())
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.boxplot([clean.loc[clean["species"] == s, "body_mass_g"] for s in species])
ax.set_xticks(range(1, len(species) + 1), species)
ax.set_xlabel("Species")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Body mass of penguins by species.





The box plot shows the same pattern and adds the spread. The Adelie and Chinstrap boxes overlap almost completely, while the Gentoo box sits well above both, with little overlap. So the difference isn’t just in the averages; most individual Gentoos are heavier than most individual penguins of the other species.

title: Penguins in Python
text:
Conclusion
Body mass separates the species into two groups: Gentoo penguins, which are much heavier, and Adelie and Chinstrap penguins, which are about the same weight. The difference is large compared to the variation within each species. A natural next step would be to check whether this holds for both sexes, since males tend to be heavier than females.

title: About
text: I grew up in Vancouver, BC, and studied Environmental Science at UBC, graduating in 2026. Along the way I worked as an Impact Assessment Officer with Environment and Climate Change Canada and as a Student Research Assistant with Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, where I spent a lot of time in the field — soil sampling, gas analysis, and processing samples in the lab. That work gave me a good feel for how messy real environmental data can be before it’s ready for any kind of analysis.

title: About
text:
Why Data Science
During my degree, courses like Hydrology and GIS were the ones I looked forward to most — not because of the environmental content alone, but because of the tools: R, RStudio, and working with data sets to answer real questions. I noticed I was more excited about the data analysis than the field component, which pushed me to look for a program that would let me build that side of my skill set properly. The MDS program seemed like the perfect place to gain more technical skills before jumping into the workforce.
